ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 2 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Dorothea Lange

code.originalText: Diagnosis of post-polio syndrome with the neuromuscular rehabilitation consultation the same day; bone density and spirometry

text.paragraph: Results of the nerve and muscle tests; neuromuscular consultation this morning. [S]

Ms. Lange returns 16 days after presenting with about 18 months of new fatigue, slowly increasing weakness of the left leg and both shoulders as well as her polio-affected right leg, aching after field work, and two falls. Her blood tests at the first visit excluded the common other causes: hemoglobin 13.1, TSH 2.1, HbA1c 5.4 percent, B12 512, creatinine 0.7, ESR 12, and CRP 0.3 were normal; creatine kinase was mildly raised at 228 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D low at 22. Her PHQ-9 was 6. Nerve conduction studies a week ago were normal, and the needle EMG showed chronic reinnervation in the right leg and, more mildly, in the left thigh and right shoulder, with no myopathy. She saw Dr. Haddad-Sorensen this morning, who confirmed post-polio syndrome. Today she had a bone density scan and spirometry. Her heartburn is much better after two weeks of omeprazole. She asked plainly whether this would keep getting worse and whether she would have to stop working in the field. [S]

list.item:
Post-polio syndrome (G14). She meets the modified March of Dimes criteria: paralytic polio in childhood confirmed by history, examination, and EMG; partial recovery followed by five decades of stable function; gradual new weakness and fatigue for more than a year; and other causes excluded by normal nerve conduction, no myopathy on EMG, and normal thyroid, blood count, glucose, B12, and inflammatory markers. The mildly raised creatine kinase fits muscle overuse. Mild depressive symptoms are a response to the fatigue, not its cause. She was told that post-polio syndrome usually progresses slowly, that pacing, the right exercise, and an orthosis often stabilize or improve function, and that field work can continue with changes. [S]
Twelve weeks of supervised non-fatiguing exercise with rest days, then a home program.
Pacing and energy conservation for field days: a lighter camera on a harness, a seat stick, an assistant to carry the tripod, and a rest day after each field day.
Custom lightweight carbon-fiber right ankle-foot orthosis and a cane in the left hand.
Home overnight oximetry because her sleep is unrefreshing.
Sedation and anesthesia precautions recorded in the chart.

Osteoporosis of the right hip, with vitamin D insufficiency (M81.8). Right femoral neck T-score -2.7, left -1.6, lumbar spine -1.8; no vertebral fracture. Disuse of the polio-affected leg lowers bone density on that side, and with two falls her fracture risk is high (FRAX about 16 percent major and 4.5 percent hip). PTH, alkaline phosphatase, phosphate, magnesium, and calcium are normal; vitamin D is low. An oral bisphosphonate is not a good choice while she has reflux symptoms. [S]
Vitamin D3 2000 units daily now.
Zoledronic acid 5 mg intravenously once vitamin D is replete, at the next visit.
24-hour urine calcium before the infusion.
Calcium from food, about 1200 mg a day.

Falls (Z91.81). Two falls from catching the right foot; foot drop and quadriceps weakness are the main causes. [S]
Orthosis and cane as above; gait and balance training.
Home changes: rails on the garden path, night lights, no loose rugs.

Heartburn on an omeprazole trial (R12). Responding after two weeks; no alarm features. [S]
Complete eight weeks, then stop and review.
